analogy.p: Macbeth is like a climber who sees the summit and cuts through the safety rope to reach it faster. The first step upward feels like triumph, but with each foot higher there is less to hold on to and more to fear. The analogy shows that the fall comes from the choice to give up his protection (loyalty, conscience, friends). It breaks down because a climber is only risking himself, whereas Macbeth drags a whole country down with him.
analogy.t: A climber who cuts his own rope

bullets: Examiners reward you for linking his decline to a **cause** (ambition, suggestion, fear) and not simply narrating what happens next.
The play is built as a steep rise and a steeper fall: he gains the crown early, and the rest of the play is the price of keeping it.
His **moral standing** and his **power** move in opposite directions after Act 2, which is the heart of the tragic irony.
The Jacobean audience believed regicide broke the divine order, so his fall would feel both deserved and inevitable.

callouts.p: A character of high status, admirable in some way, whose flaw (hamartia) and choices lead to their downfall and often their death, arousing pity and fear in the audience.

The strongest answers argue about this tension: the witches seem to offer fate, but Macbeth chooses to act on the prophecy. He even tries to force it by murdering Duncan rather than waiting to see if chance will crown him.

core.h: What a tragic arc is and why Macbeth fits it
core.p: A tragedy follows a person of high status whose fatal weakness leads to a fall that is partly their own fault. Shakespeare asks the audience to feel **pity** because the protagonist is admirable at the start, and **fear** because we recognise how easily choices can lead to disaster. Macbeth is unusual because he is not a simple victim of fate: the witches predict, but they never tell him to kill, and every crucial decision is his own. That makes the play a study of how a good man corrupts himself.

Notice that the sympathy we feel is greatest at the two ends of the play. In Act 2 his conscience still works; in Act 5 he is stripped of everything and still fights. The middle is where we are most appalled.

head: Act and scene
Macbeth's state
Key moment
What the audience feels
rows: Celebrated hero, then curious and uneasy
Praised as “brave Macbeth”; starts at the prophecy; imagines murder
Hides his “black and deep desires”; debates and nearly abandons the plan
The dagger vision; the murder; Duncan's body found
Plans Banquo's death; the ghost at the feast
Visits the witches; orders the Macduff massacre
“Tomorrow” soliloquy; refuses to yield; killed by Macduff

bullets: His first line, “So foul and fair a day I have not seen”, echoes the witches' paradox “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” and links him to them before they meet.
In 1.3 his aside about the “horrid image” of murder, with a heart that pounds, shows imagination and physical dread: he is horrified by his own mind.
In 1.4 he sees Malcolm named Prince of Cumberland as an obstacle and asks the stars to “hide your fires”: ambition now requires darkness and concealment.
In 1.5 Lady Macbeth says he is too full of “the milk of human kindness” to take the shortcut. She sees both his ambition and his conscience.
In 1.7 he lists the reasons not to kill Duncan (kinsman, subject, host) and admits he has only “vaulting ambition”. The moral argument is lost by his own admission.

callouts.p: Act 1 is built on contrast: the bloody battlefield (1.2), the supernatural (1.3), the polite court (1.4), the Macbeth castle (1.6) and then the private debate (1.7). Each scene tightens the trap and moves him from public hero to private plotter.

core.h: Act 1: the hero who is already tempted
core.p: Shakespeare introduces Macbeth through other people's praise before we see him, so that his later fall has height to fall from. The captain describes him cutting a man “from the nave to th' chops”, a gruesome image that shows violence is already his profession. Yet this violence is channelled into loyalty. The key moment is 1.3: when the witches hail him as king, Banquo notices that Macbeth seems to “start” and fear things that “sound so fair”. The fear shows that the thought of murder was already in his mind.

bullets: The guilt is shown through his senses: sounds, sights, and the sticky blood on his hands.
The imagery of “the multitudinous seas incarnadine” turns his guilt into something so vast that it would stain the ocean.
After Duncan, he performs grief in 2.3 and kills the grooms, an impulsive second murder that already shows the tyrant.
In 3.1 he is king but admits “To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus”. Possession of the crown brings fear, not satisfaction.
In 3.2 he tells Lady Macbeth that “full of scorpions is my mind” and calls her “dearest chuck”, keeping the plan for Banquo secret. The partnership is breaking.
In 3.4 the ghost at the banquet shows his guilt breaking into public view, and he admits “I am in blood / Stepped in so far” that returning would be as hard as going on.
core.h: Acts 2 and 3: murder and the turn into tyranny
core.p: Act 2 is the moral centre of the play. The dagger soliloquy (2.1) shows him hallucinating the weapon he will use, and the murder itself happens offstage so the audience sees only its psychological aftermath. In 2.2 he cannot say “Amen” and he fears that the blood on his hands cannot be washed clean. The sentence “Macbeth does murder sleep” is the key idea: by killing a sleeping king he has destroyed his own capacity for peace.

head: Moment
Language
Effect
rows: Shows a divided, imaginative mind; guilt before the act
Short, broken lines; fixation on hands and sleep
Cold, clipped orders; paired with image of “scorpions”
Broken, defensive speech to the empty seat
Public collapse of his kingly mask

bullets: The massacre in 4.2 is his lowest moral point because the victims are a mother and children who pose no threat; the audience's sympathy is exhausted.
In 5.3 he says his way of life is “fall'n into the sere, the yellow leaf” and that he cannot expect “honour, love, obedience, troops of friends”. He understands what he has traded away.
In 5.5, hearing of Lady Macbeth's death, he responds “She should have died hereafter”. The line is ambiguous: it can express numb exhaustion, or grief too painful to face.
The “Tomorrow, and tomorrow” soliloquy reduces life to a “walking shadow” and a “tale / Told by an idiot”: his earlier poetry has become nihilism.
In 5.8 he learns Macduff was “untimely ripped” from his mother's womb and accuses the witches of being “juggling fiends”, yet refuses to yield and dies fighting.

callouts.p: His final courage is real, but he fights from pride not repentance: “I will not yield / To kiss the ground”. A strong answer holds both ideas: he regains some dignity but never regains his conscience.
callouts.t: Do not call it a redemption

core.h: Acts 4 and 5: false security, isolation and collapse
core.p: In 4.1 Macbeth seeks out the witches himself, reversing the earlier meeting where they sought him. The apparitions flatter him into believing he is invulnerable, and he decides “The very firstlings of my heart” will be “The firstlings of my hand”. This marks a loss of reflection: he will now act on impulse before thought, which leads directly to the massacre of Macduff's family. By Act 5 he is surrounded by enemies and deserted by thanes, yet he keeps a bleak courage.

bullets: **Early**: extended metaphors (“vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself”), questions, hesitations, hypotheticals (“If it were done when 'tis done”).
**Middle**: commands and short assertions, imagery of blood, beasts and scorpions, with ideas of safety dominating.
**Late**: flat, repetitive, rhythmic language (“Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow”) conveying the exhaustion of a man who sees time as meaningless.
**Soliloquies** give us access to his mind. Pay attention to how they change from deliberation (1.7) to horror (2.1) to calculation (3.1) to despair (5.5).
**Imagery patterns**: darkness for concealment, blood for guilt, clothing (“borrowed robes”) for usurped status, sleep for innocence and peace.

callouts.p: The play compresses the time between the murder and the collapse: after Act 2 things happen rapidly. Link that pace to his statement that he is “in blood / Stepped in so far”: one crime forces another with increasing speed.

fig.cap: The relationship between Macbeth and Lady Macbeth reverses. She drives the early decisions; he drives everything after Act 3 and leaves her behind.

core.h: How his language charts the decline
core.p: Early Macbeth speaks in rich, imaginative blank verse full of metaphor and darkness, because his conscience is active and his mind teems with possible futures. As the play proceeds his speech becomes blunter, more brutal, and finally empty. This stylistic change is itself evidence of the tragic arc, and showing it gains AO2 credit.

bullets: **Victim of manipulation**: the witches tempt, Lady Macbeth taunts his manhood, and Duncan's naming of Malcolm as heir blocks his path. He is pushed along.
**Author of his own fall**: he alone speaks the “vaulting ambition” speech and chooses to kill. No one forces his hand in Acts 3 and 4.
**Imaginative man destroyed by his imagination**: the same mind that makes him a poet also makes him suffer. We pity him because he knows what he is doing.
**Jacobean providential view**: God punishes regicide and restores order through Malcolm and Macduff. The ending is not only personal, it is cosmic.
**Modern psychological view**: ambition, guilt, insomnia and paranoia can be read as the story of a man whose conscience cannot be silenced.

callouts.p: Do not say it is “tragic because he dies”. Say it is tragic because a man of real quality destroys everything of value in himself, and recognises it too late.

core.h: Why do we still feel pity? Interpretations to offer
core.p: Grade 9 answers do not settle for one view of Macbeth. They explore how the play can be read in more than one way and test each against the evidence. The strongest approach is to argue that Shakespeare makes Macbeth both culpable and sympathetic, and that this double response is the tragedy.

bullets: Never write “In Jacobean times people believed...” as a stand-alone sentence: link it to a quotation and an effect.
Use the Great Chain to explain why the natural world breaks down in 2.3 and 2.4, and why the arc is a cosmic as well as personal fall.

callouts.p: Say “many Jacobeans” or “the Jacobean audience may have viewed”, not “everyone believed”. Overclaiming about the past is a common AO3 slip.

core.h: Context: AO3 hooks that strengthen the arc
core.p: Context must be woven into your argument and used to explain a choice Shakespeare makes. For Macbeth the most useful contexts are the Jacobean belief in the divine right of kings, the Great Chain of Being, King James I's interest in witchcraft, and the recent Gunpowder Plot of 1605.

head: Context fact
How it shapes Macbeth's arc
Where to use it
rows: Divine right of kings: the monarch was God's representative
Killing Duncan is not only murder but a sin against heaven, so his guilt and the natural disorder that follows are inevitable
2.2 to 2.4: the night of unnatural events
Moving a subject above his rightful place disrupts the order of nature; the tragic arc is the restoring of that order
The fall in Act 5; Malcolm's final speech
James I wrote Daemonologie (1597) and was interested in witches
The witches would be a serious threat to the audience; Macbeth's dealings with them are dangerous and damning
Treachery and regicide were fresh fears; a play showing a regicide punished flatters the king
Macbeth was written for the Jacobean stage (about 1606)
Audiences expected tragedy to restore order, so the ending is satisfying for them

bullets: **Step 1**: Underline the key word in the question (ambition, guilt, tyrant, hero).

**Step 2**: Write a conceptual thesis that makes an argument about the arc, such as: Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a man whose imagination makes him both capable of ambition and unable to escape its consequences.
**Step 3**: Plan four or five points in chronological order, with one quotation in each and one technique or structural comment.
**Step 4**: In each paragraph, zoom in on a single word, zoom out to the play's structure, then link to purpose and context.
**Step 5**: Finish with an evaluative conclusion about what Shakespeare wants the audience to learn.

callouts.p: Check how the marks are shared on your paper. Keep AO4 in mind: spelling and punctuation are assessed on the Shakespeare question, so proofread character names, “Duncan”, “Banquo”, “Macduff”, and the word “tyrant”.

core.h: Exam technique: writing about the whole arc
core.p: Questions on Macbeth often ask how Shakespeare presents ambition, guilt, power or Macbeth himself. In part (a) the focus is on the extract and you should place it on the arc. In part (b) you use recalled quotations from elsewhere in the play, so build a bank of short key phrases for each stage of his decline.

plan: Establish his heroism and the hint of temptation in Act 1
The 1.7 and 2.1 soliloquies as proof of free will
The murder and its psychological cost
Act 3: security demands more violence and the partnership breaks
Act 5: emptiness, recognition, and defiant dignity
essays.q: How does Shakespeare present Macbeth's journey from hero to tyrant? (Part (b) style: use your knowledge of the whole play.)
essays.text:
Shakespeare opens with a Macbeth whose heroism is established by report. The captain's praise of “brave Macbeth” gives us an ideal, so that when the witches hail him in 1.3 we notice his reaction: he “starts” at prophecies that “sound so fair”. The verb implies that temptation finds an existing impulse, and this is the first sign that his flaw is internal. The prophecy does not create ambition; it names it.

The soliloquy in 1.7 then makes his responsibility explicit. Here he lists every reason against murder (kinsman, subject, host) and concludes that he has nothing to drive him but “vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself”. The metaphor of a rider jumping too far diagnoses his own flaw and also predicts his fall. Crucially, the speech breaks off mid-line, as if his argument collapses under its own weight, and Lady Macbeth enters to finish it. A Jacobean audience, schooled to see the king as God's deputy, would see that he knows what he does is sacrilege, which turns later sympathy into complicated judgement.

In Act 2 Shakespeare turns the language inward. The “dagger of the mind, a false creation” shows an intelligent man watching himself walk into delusion. After the murder, the voice that cries “Macbeth does murder sleep” is the first sign that guilt will not let him rest. The use of his own name in the third person suggests a self already split into doer and witness. The cost is not punishment from others but a mind permanently on edge.

The turn from hero to tyrant comes in Act 3, where the structure shows how one crime forces another. As king, he declares “To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus”: possession of the crown brings fear, not fulfilment. That fear leads to Banquo's murder and, in 3.2, the phrase “dearest chuck” shows him excluding Lady Macbeth from the plot. The affectionate nickname masks an increasingly cold, controlling voice. By 3.4 he admits “I am in blood / Stepped in so far”, and the verb “stepped” suggests not a leap but a series of choices, making him the author of his own predicament. Shakespeare may be suggesting that evil is a process rather than a moment.

By Act 5 the poetry has collapsed into emptiness. “She should have died hereafter” can be read as callous or as grief too deep to face, and this ambiguity is the point: Shakespeare lets us hold pity and condemnation at once. In the “Tomorrow” soliloquy, life is “a walking shadow”, a performance with no meaning, a sentiment that also reminds the audience of the theatre they sit in. Yet he does not repent. His final defiance, “I will not yield”, reclaims warrior dignity without regaining moral worth. For a Jacobean audience, the restoration of order under Malcolm is a triumph of providence; for a modern audience, the haunting element is that the destroyer was once so admirable. Shakespeare's purpose is therefore double: to warn against the price of unchecked ambition and to show how vulnerable even the best minds are to their own desires.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare presents Macbeth's journey as a tragedy of self-corruption, in which a man of remarkable imagination and courage uses those same gifts to destroy himself, so that the audience is forced to pity the hero even as it condemns the tyrant.
why: AO1: a conceptual thesis (self-corruption) controls the whole argument and quotations are short, embedded and chronological.
AO2: zooms in on single words (“starts”, “stepped”, “dearest chuck”) and comments on structure (the broken line in 1.7, the soliloquy in 5.5).
AO3: context is used to explain audience response (divine right, providence) rather than being bolted on.
Offers more than one reading (“callous or grief too deep”) and evaluates writer's purpose in the conclusion.

model: Macbeth carefully lists reasons against murder: kinsman, subject, host
The metaphor “vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself” shows self-knowledge
He fears judgement, even “here, upon this bank and shoal of time”
Soliloquy form gives access to his private mind; hesitations and conditionals show conflict
The broken final line suggests his argument collapses
Link to the rest of the play: awareness yet choice makes his fall tragic
Context: regicide as sacrilege in Jacobean belief
exam.q: Starting with this speech (Act 1 Scene 7, “If it were done when 'tis done”), explain how far you think Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a man who is aware of the consequences of his ambition. (Part (a) style; check the marks on your paper, around 20.)
exam.tip: AO2 marks come from words and structure inside the extract. Do not drift into the whole play; keep a thread back to “how far”.

model: Define the tragic hero and apply to Macbeth
Early heroism: “brave Macbeth”
Hamartia: ambition plus susceptibility
His conscience: dagger soliloquy and “sleep”
Peripeteia: from triumphant king to isolated tyrant in Acts 3 to 5
Anagnorisis: “Tomorrow” soliloquy and “juggling fiends”
Context: divine right, order restored by Malcolm
exam.q: Explain how Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a tragic hero. Refer to the whole play. (Part (b) style; check the marks on your paper.)
exam.tip: Use only short quotations. The best answers argue why the play is tragic, not simply that he dies.

model: Hallucinations: the dagger and later Banquo's ghost show his mind cannot rest
Sleep imagery: “Macbeth does murder sleep” shows loss of peace
Blood on hands: “multitudinous seas incarnadine” shows guilt cannot be washed away
Short broken sentences after the murder show shock and mental strain
exam.q: Explain two ways Shakespeare shows Macbeth's guilt after Duncan's murder. (4 marks)
exam.tip: Two clear points with a short quotation and an explanation each; do not write a paragraph about plot.

model: Act 1: praised as “brave”, loyal and imaginative
Act 1: guilt and doubt in “vaulting ambition” speech
Act 5: numb, exhausted, “She should have died hereafter”
Act 5: sees life as “a walking shadow”
His language moves from rich metaphor to bleak repetition
He still fights with courage (“I will not yield”), so change is partial
exam.q: How does Macbeth change between Act 1 and Act 5? Use one quotation from each end of the play. (6 marks)
exam.tip: Contrast must be explicit: “whereas at the start... by the end...”. Show change, not just two descriptions.

model: Macbeth confronted by the ghost speaks in broken, hysterical lines
“I am in blood / Stepped in so far” suggests entrapment
Lady Macbeth's interruptions show the partnership strain
The ghost is a symbol of guilt and the return of a repressed past
The banquet is a public occasion, so private guilt breaks into the political world
Structure: the feast is the high point of his power and the start of his collapse
exam.q: Starting with this extract (Act 3 Scene 4), how does Shakespeare present Macbeth's state of mind? (Part (a) style)
exam.tip: AO2 focus: language of fear and the stage action (ghost, empty chair).

model: Victim: witches' prophecy, Lady Macbeth's pressure, Duncan's naming of Malcolm
Villain: free will in 1.7, the murders of Duncan's guards, Banquo, the Macduffs
Imagination makes him suffer: scorpions, ghost, sleep
Audience sympathy at the end vs. moral judgement
Context: Jacobeans would see regicide as unforgivable, but also see him tempted by the devil
Conclusion: Shakespeare creates a tragic hero who is both
exam.q: “Macbeth is more a victim than a villain.” To what extent do you agree? (Part (b) style)
exam.tip: Pick a clear line of argument in your thesis and test the opposite view with “although” or “however”.

mistakes.r: Explain the cause and effect behind each stage and attach a short quotation and analysis to each: the arc is an argument, not a story.
mistakes.w: Narrating the plot: “Then Macbeth kills Duncan and then he kills Banquo...”

mistakes.r: Argue that they offer prophecy, not instruction, and that Macbeth's response shows his own ambition and free will.
mistakes.w: Saying the witches make Macbeth kill Duncan.

mistakes.r: Show that Shakespeare establishes his heroism first (“brave Macbeth”) so that the fall is tragic and the audience can feel pity.
mistakes.w: Calling him a villain from the very start.

mistakes.r: Define the term in context and link hamartia and peripeteia to specific scenes.
mistakes.w: Using “tragic hero” without definition or evidence.

mistakes.r: Discuss the “Tomorrow” soliloquy and his defiance to show complexity: a tyrant who recognises emptiness and still fights.
mistakes.w: Ignoring Act 4 and Act 5, or treating the end as pure justice.

mistakes.r: Link divine right to a specific moment, such as the unnatural night after Duncan's murder, and say what it makes the audience feel.
mistakes.w: Context bolted on: “In Jacobean times kings were important”.

mistakes.r: Use short embedded quotations of a few words and zoom in on individual words such as “vaulting” or “stepped”.
mistakes.w: Quoting a whole speech and then paraphrasing it.

mistakes.r: Offer at least two readings (numb grief or callousness) and say which is more convincing and why.
mistakes.w: Missing alternative interpretations of key lines like “She should have died hereafter”.

quotes.a: The captain's adjective establishes Macbeth as a loyal hero before he appears. “Brave” is later ironic when he commits cowardly murder. Hearing him praised first means the audience has an ideal against which to measure his decline, intensifying the tragedy.
quotes.c: A Jacobean audience valued loyalty in war; his early heroism makes his later treachery to the crown more shocking.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 2, early in the scene
quotes.t: Epithet, dramatic irony, characterisation by report

quotes.a: Macbeth echoes the witches' paradox from the opening scene without having heard it, suggesting an uncanny link between him and the supernatural. The antithesis also captures the day's double nature: victory in battle and the beginning of temptation.
quotes.c: Jacobean audiences believed evil could work on those already inclined to listen.
quotes.q: So foul and fair a day
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 3, early in the scene

quotes.a: The adjectives connect his ambition to darkness and depth, suggesting that it is both hidden and bottomless. His wish that the stars “hide your fires” shows that he knows his thoughts are shameful and must be concealed from heaven.
quotes.c: Darkness was associated with sin and evil; he is asking nature to conspire in regicide.
quotes.t: Imagery of darkness, personification of stars, aside

quotes.a: The horse-riding metaphor suggests ambition that jumps too far and falls on the other side. The speech ends abruptly in mid-line, as if Macbeth runs out of reasons. It is both a diagnosis of his flaw and a prediction of his fall.
quotes.c: The audience knows regicide upsets the divine order, so he is aware of the cost.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 7, closing lines of the soliloquy

quotes.a: He recognises the vision as imaginary, yet still follows it. The phrase shows an intelligent man, aware of his own delusion, moving towards the deed. The sense of being guided by a floating blade also hints at supernatural pressure.
quotes.c: Visions could be read by a Jacobean audience as a sign of supernatural or demonic influence on a troubled mind.
quotes.q: dagger of the mind, a false creation

quotes.a: The imagined voice announces that he has killed sleep itself, the symbol of innocence and rest. The third person suggests he is already splitting from himself. The line anticipates his insomnia and Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking.
quotes.c: Killing a sleeping king doubled the sin of regicide, as it destroyed both a ruler and a guest.
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 2, shortly after the murder

quotes.a: The metaphor presents guilt as a swarm of stinging creatures that constantly attack him from within. The plural “scorpions” suggests numerous, painful thoughts and the impossibility of rest. It also helps explain why he moves on to further violence.
quotes.c: Venom and serpent imagery recurs in the play (Lady Macbeth's “serpent under't”), linking guilt to corruption and betrayal.
quotes.q: full of scorpions is my mind
quotes.ref: Act 3 Sc 2, early in the scene
quotes.t: Metaphor, plosive “c” sounds, imagery of venom

quotes.a: He compares his situation to wading through a river of blood, so far in that going back is as hard as going on. The word “stepped” suggests a series of deliberate choices and not a single fall, reinforcing his responsibility. The line captures the tragic logic of the play.
quotes.c: Macbeth himself says that “blood will have blood”, voicing the Jacobean assumption that murder is answered by divine justice.
quotes.q: I am in blood / Stepped in so far
quotes.ref: Act 3 Sc 4, late in the scene

quotes.a: The line is deliberately ambiguous. It can mean that her death will come at a better time, or that he cannot take in the news now. The reaction is short, flat and emotionally numb, showing how far he has moved from the sensitive man of Act 1.
quotes.c: He is heirless, so a throne won by murder leads nowhere; the loss of his wife strips him of his last close bond.
quotes.ref: Act 5 Sc 5, after the cry of women

quotes.a: He reduces life to a shadow and a “poor player” who struts briefly and disappears. The metaphor from theatre reflects the audience's own situation and makes his despair universal. The rhythm of repeated “tomorrow” slows the verse, reproducing a feeling of endless, empty time.
quotes.c: The Jacobean theatre's self-awareness (the Globe) lets Shakespeare remind us that the “tragedy” is a performance.

quotes.a: Despite knowing the prophecies have betrayed him, he refuses to surrender to Malcolm. The statement restores some of his old warrior's dignity, but it is also a mark of pride: he will die rather than be humiliated. Audiences are left with pity and judgement together.
quotes.c: Dying in battle was seen as an honourable end for a warrior, even though he dies as a usurper.
quotes.ref: Act 5 Sc 8, late in the scene

summary: Trace Macbeth from celebrated war hero to isolated tyrant and be able to explain how Shakespeare shapes this tragic arc through language, structure, soliloquy and the Jacobean context, so that you can write about his development at any point in the play.

terms.d: The fatal flaw or error of judgement in a tragic hero that causes their downfall; in Macbeth, ambition combined with a readiness to be persuaded.
A sudden reversal of fortune; Macbeth moves from triumphant king to hunted tyrant.
The moment of recognition when the hero realises the truth about themselves or their situation.
A speech in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud when alone on stage, giving direct access to their mind.
When the audience knows something a character does not, such as the truth about Duncan's fate when he arrives at the castle.
The emotional release an audience feels at the end of a tragedy, after pity and fear.
A ruler who seizes or keeps power by force and rules through fear and violence.
Hints early in the play of events to come, such as the unnatural weather and “Fair is foul”.
Unrhymed iambic pentameter, the usual form for noble characters in Shakespeare; its irregularities show mental strain.
Someone who takes a position of power, especially a throne, by force and without right.
